unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 10 gathers the whole of Grade 6 into one researched capstone project. You revise thirty review words drawn from Units 1 to 8, from illegal, citizen and instrument to conduction, rehearsal and apprentice. Six grammar workshops bring back the tenses, the first conditional, relative clauses, precise description, reported speech and the final editing skills of the year. You then reread five review texts, plan and draft a multi-section English product for a defined audience, defend it, answer questions and reflect on how far you have grown.
unit.learningPath:
Reread the five review texts and answer the twelve comprehension questions.
Revise the thirty review words and build your research word map, unit by unit.
Work through the six grammar workshops, one target at a time.
Plan, draft and improve a researched multi-section product for a real audience.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, rehearse across them and deliver your four-minute presentation there — this is optional. If you are learning independently, rehearse and record your four-minute presentation on your own or with your family instead.
Defend your conclusions, then finish with the capstone quiz, the portfolio assignment and your Grade 7 reflection.
howToUse: This is your capstone: one project that draws on the whole year. There is no video — start by reading the project page.
The five readings are review texts, one from each of Units 1 to 5. Reread them and answer the twelve comprehension questions.

In Writing you plan, draft and improve a researched multi-section product for a real audience. In Speaking you rehearse a four-minute presentation and defend your conclusions — record it if you have no live sessions.
The Final course quiz is on this page, after every section has a tick. It is extra — it does not lock the unit.

readings.title: Review text 1: The Weaver and the Wind (Unit 1)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In a small village near the coast, there lived a woman named Dina who was known across the whole region for her extraordinary skill at weaving. Her cloths were so beautiful that merchants travelled from distant towns just to buy them. The patterns she created were unlike anything anyone had ever seen, with swirling designs of deep blue and gold that seemed to shimmer in the sunlight. People often said that Dina's fingers moved as if they were guided by the wind itself.
Dina was proud of her talent, and she guarded her methods very closely. Whenever younger women in the village asked her to teach them her techniques, she always refused. "These skills took me many years to master," she would say, shaking her head firmly. "Why should I simply give them away? My knowledge is the very thing that makes my cloth so valuable."
Her neighbour was an elderly man named Zane, who often watched her work from his doorstep. He had lived in the village his whole life, and everyone respected him for his patience and wisdom. "Dina," he said gently one morning, stepping a little closer to her loom, "a river that refuses to share its water slowly becomes a swamp. It grows stale, and in the end it turns useless."
"I am no river, Uncle," Dina replied, with a polite but dismissive smile. "I am more like a deep well, and my water is meant for my own family alone. I have worked hard to fill it, and I will not let strangers take from it." Zane shook his head sadly, but he said nothing more, for he had learned long ago that people must discover certain truths for themselves.
One evening, dark clouds gathered along the horizon. The monsoon winds arrived far earlier than anyone had expected, howling through the village with tremendous force. Dina rushed outside to protect her precious loom, but the wind was simply too powerful for her. It tore through her workshop like a wild animal, snapping the wooden frame and scattering her finest silk threads across the muddy ground. The heavy rain that followed soaked everything it touched. By morning, her workshop lay in ruins, and her loom, her thread, and her finished cloths had all been destroyed.
Dina sat among the wreckage with tears streaming down her face. She had no money to replace her loom, and the silk merchants would not return for many long months. Without her weaving, she had no way to earn a living for her family. For the very first time in her whole life, she felt completely helpless.

readings.title: Review text 2: Training Champions - The Science Behind Sport (Unit 2)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In many communities across East Africa and around the world, sport has always been more than a game. From the long-distance runners of the highlands to busy basketball courts and football pitches, physical activity brings people together and keeps them strong. But have you ever wondered what happens inside your body when you exercise? The answer involves fascinating biological processes that scientists still study today.
When you run, swim or play football, your muscles need more energy, so your heart beats faster to pump blood around your body. This blood carries oxygen to your muscles so they can keep working. If you train regularly, your heart will become stronger and more efficient. It will pump more blood with each beat, which means it does not have to work as hard while you rest. This is why trained athletes often have lower resting heart rates than people who never exercise.
Nutrition matters too. If you eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit, vegetables and whole grains, your body will have the fuel it needs to perform well. Protein from foods such as beans, lentils, eggs and fish helps your muscles repair and grow after exercise. If you do not eat enough healthy food, your performance will deteriorate over time. Harmful bacteria can enter your body through unclean food or water, so good hygiene is an important part of staying healthy.
Water is just as important as food. When you exercise, your body loses water through sweat, and if you do not drink enough, you may feel tired, dizzy or unwell. The environmental conditions matter as well: if the weather is very hot, athletes must take extra care to stay cool and avoid heat exhaustion.
Sleep is another vital part of any athlete's routine. During sleep the body repairs itself, muscles rebuild, and the brain sorts through everything it has learned during the day. If a young athlete does not get enough sleep, their reaction times will slow and their concentration will suffer. Most experts say children need between nine and eleven hours of sleep each night.
East Africa's high, cool highlands have produced many of the world's greatest long-distance runners, such as Mo Farah and Tegla Loroupe. These champions did not succeed by talent alone. They trained with discipline, ate well, rested properly and listened to their coaches. Across history, many different cultures have prized physical skills like swimming, running, riding and archery, treating a healthy body as something to value and protect.
Sport also teaches life skills. If you play in a team, you will learn to cooperate, communicate clearly and handle both victory and defeat with grace. In a multicultural society, sport is one of the most powerful ways to bring different people together. Remember this: if you take care of your body today, it will take care of you tomorrow.

readings.title: Review text 3: The Web of Life (Unit 3)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
East Africa is a region which stretches from the dry plains of Somalia to the green highlands of Ethiopia and the vast savannahs of Kenya and Tanzania. It is home to one of the richest collections of wildlife on Earth. Every animal, plant, and insect plays a part in the great web of life. Scientists call this web an ecosystem — a community of living things that depend on each other and on the land, water, and air around them.
At the heart of every ecosystem lies the food chain. A food chain shows who eats whom. It begins with plants, which use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. These plants are called producers because they produce the energy that the entire chain depends on. In the semi-arid grasslands of the Horn of Africa, tough grasses and thorny acacia trees are the main producers. They endure months of dry heat and burst into life when the rains finally come, feeding the animals that graze across the plains.
Understanding this web begins with a few important words. A habitat is the natural home of an animal or plant, and a species is a group of living things of the same kind. Some creatures are predators, which hunt other animals for food, while their prey are the animals that are hunted. As you read the passages in this unit, watch for these words, and notice how each writer uses the present simple tense to state facts that are always true. Notice, too, the relative clauses — small groups of words beginning with who, which, or where — that add extra detail about the animals and places being described.
The natural world of East Africa is both beautiful and fragile. Every grassland, river, and coral reef depends on a careful balance, and that balance is easier to break than it looks. When one species disappears, the animals that depend on it can suffer too, and the effects can spread right along the food chain. As you learn how food chains and ecosystems work, you will also discover why protecting them matters for every family and community that shares the land, water, and air of this remarkable region.

readings.title: Review text 4: Inventions That Changed Everyday Life (Unit 4)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
For thousands of years, human beings have solved problems by inventing new tools and machines. Some inventions were simple, like the wheel or the needle, but they changed life forever. Others were complex, like the printing press or the electric generator, and they opened doors that nobody had imagined before.
One of the most important inventions in history was the compass. Before the compass existed, sailors relied on the stars for navigation. If clouds covered the sky, ships lost their way. Chinese inventors created the first magnetic compass over a thousand years ago. Once sailors had this tool, they explored new territories, crossed dangerous straits, and connected civilizations that had never met before. The compass did not just change travel; it changed the way humans understood the whole world.
Another invention that transformed daily life was the printing press. In the year 1440, a German inventor named Johannes Gutenberg proposed a machine that could print books quickly. Before his invention, every book was copied by hand, which took months. The printing press made books cheaper and easier to produce. Within a few decades, millions of people who had never owned a book could finally read and learn. Knowledge was no longer something only the elite controlled; it belonged to everyone.
In the modern era, the electric generator changed how people lived and worked. A generator converts movement into electricity. Once communities had electricity, they could light their homes, power machines, and store food safely. In many parts of East Africa and the wider world, generators still provide power to schools, hospitals, and homes that are not connected to the main electricity grid. A single generator can make the difference between a community that struggles in the dark and one that thrives with light.
Today, young inventors continue to solve real problems. In Kenya, a teenager invented a device that keeps lions away from livestock by using flashing lights. In Somalia, students have built simple solar-powered chargers so that families in rural areas can charge their phones. These inventions show that you do not need a big laboratory or a lot of money to make a difference; you need curiosity, creativity, and commitment.
Every great invention started with a question: What if? What if we could fly? What if we could talk to someone on the other side of the world? What if we could make clean water from the sea? The inventors who changed history did not have all the answers. They had the courage to ask questions, try new ideas, and learn from their mistakes. That is the true procedure of invention: observe, question, experiment, and improve. And it is a procedure that anyone, including you, can follow.

readings.title: Review text 5: Money, Markets and Making Good Choices (Unit 5)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every morning in cities and towns across East Africa, markets come alive. Stalls are set up with colourful fabrics, fresh fruit, and bags of rice and sugar. Shopkeepers call out prices. Customers count their coins carefully. A woman buys enough flour for the week. A boy saves his last few shillings instead of buying sweets. A grandmother bargains firmly for a fair price on vegetables. Money moves from hand to hand, and each decision — big or small — tells a story about how people think about value.
But what is money, really? Money is a tool. It is not good or bad on its own. What matters is how we use it. Financial literacy means understanding how money works and learning to make smart choices with it. This includes knowing the difference between needs and wants. A need is something you must have to live safely and healthily, like food, clean water, shelter, and clothing. A want is something nice to have but not essential, like a new toy, a fancy phone case, or extra sweets after school.
One of the most crucial money skills is saving. Saving means putting aside part of your money for the future instead of spending it all at once. Even small amounts add up over time. If you save just a few coins each week, after several months you might have enough for something substantial — a book you have wanted, a gift for someone you love, or a contribution to a family goal. Many families teach children to be balanced with money: not to waste it, not to hoard it selfishly, and to share with those who have less. A wise saying reminds us that the best people are those who are most useful to others. Giving to charity is not only generous — it is a thoughtful way of using what we have and strengthening our community.
A budget is a plan for how to use your money. Even young people can make a simple budget. Imagine you receive some pocket money each week. You could divide it into three parts: one part for saving, one part for spending on things you need or enjoy, and one part for giving to charity or helping your family. This simple plan helps you feel in control and teaches you to think carefully about your resources. People who budget well are often more productive with their money than people who spend without thinking.
Another important skill is learning to compare prices. When you go to the market with your family, you might notice that one shop sells rice more cheaply than another, or that one brand of soap lasts longer than a cheaper one. Comparing carefully means you get better value. This is a form of critical thinking — the same skill you use in school when you adapt your ideas based on new information.
Money can sometimes cause stress, especially for families who do not have much. It is important to be sensitive to this. Not everyone has the same amount, and that is nothing to feel uncomfortable about. What matters is being humble, grateful for what you have, and wise with whatever resources are available to you. A person who manages a meager income well can be far more successful than someone who wastes a large fortune.
Understanding money is a privilege and a responsibility. The earlier you start learning, the better prepared you will be. Whether you are saving for a family celebration, helping with the shopping, or simply choosing between two treats at the corner shop, every choice you make is practice for the bigger decisions ahead.

comprehension.question: What lesson does the story of Dina the weaver begin to teach?
comprehension.correctAnswer: That guarding your skill or knowledge only for yourself, like a well kept from everyone, can leave you helpless when trouble finally comes.
comprehension.explanation: Zane warns that a river which shares nothing becomes a swamp, and the storm then destroys everything Dina had guarded alone.

comprehension.question: Which detail shows how proud Dina was of her weaving skill?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She always refused to teach the younger women, saying her secret knowledge was the very thing that made her cloth valuable.
comprehension.explanation: The passage says she guarded her methods closely and would not share her techniques with anyone.

comprehension.question: According to the sport text, why does regular training help an athlete's heart?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because training makes the heart stronger and more efficient, so it pumps more blood with each beat and works less hard at rest.
comprehension.explanation: The text explains this is why trained athletes often have lower resting heart rates than people who never exercise.

comprehension.question: What does the sport passage say happens if you do not eat enough healthy food?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Your performance will deteriorate over time, because your body lacks the fuel it needs to perform well.
comprehension.explanation: The writer links a balanced diet of fruit, vegetables and whole grains to having the energy to train and compete.

comprehension.question: How does the Life in the Wild text define an ecosystem?
comprehension.correctAnswer: As a community of living things that depend on each other and on the land, water and air around them.
comprehension.explanation: The writer calls the great web of life an ecosystem near the start of the passage.

comprehension.question: Why does the wildlife text call plants the producers of a food chain?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because plants use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make their own food, producing the energy that the whole chain depends on.
comprehension.explanation: The passage says the food chain begins with plants, and that everything above them relies on the energy they make.

comprehension.question: What overall point does the inventions text make about who can invent?
comprehension.correctAnswer: That anyone with curiosity, creativity and commitment can invent, because the real procedure is to observe, question, experiment and improve.
comprehension.explanation: The passage ends by saying young inventors in Kenya and Somalia solved real problems without big laboratories or money.

comprehension.question: How did the printing press change who could read and learn?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It made books far cheaper and quicker to produce, so within decades millions who had never owned a book could finally read and learn.
comprehension.explanation: Before it, every book was copied by hand over many months, and knowledge belonged only to the elite.

comprehension.question: What is the central message of the Money Matters text?
comprehension.correctAnswer: That money is only a tool, and what really counts is making wise, balanced choices such as saving, budgeting and sharing with others.
comprehension.explanation: The passage repeats that money is not good or bad on its own; how we use it is what matters.

comprehension.question: What three parts does the money text suggest you divide pocket money into?
comprehension.correctAnswer: One part for saving, one part for spending on needs or things you enjoy, and one part for giving to charity or helping your family.
comprehension.explanation: The passage describes this simple budget as a way to feel in control of your resources.

comprehension.question: The weaver story and the money text both value wisdom; what shared idea about sharing do they express?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Both suggest that hoarding selfishly, whether it is weaving skill or money, is unwise, and that sharing with others makes a person stronger.
comprehension.explanation: Dina's guarded well fails her, while the money passage praises budgeting and giving to charity.

comprehension.question: How could the lesson from Dina the weaver guide the way you research and share your capstone project?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It reminds me to share my ideas and sources openly instead of guarding them, so my work grows rather than turning stale like a swamp.
comprehension.explanation: Zane's warning that an unshared river becomes a swamp models why sharing knowledge strengthens a learner.

grammar.title: Verb tenses across the year
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Grade 6 used several tenses, so keep each one accurate and matched to its time.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present perfect (Unit 1): "I have finished my capstone draft."
Past simple (Unit 4): "Yesterday I edited the opening."
Past continuous (Unit 7): "While I was presenting, the class listened closely."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "I have finished it yesterday" mixes two times; use the past simple with a finished-time word: "I finished it yesterday."
grammar.memoryTip: Match the tense to the time word: yesterday takes past simple, since and already take present perfect.
grammar.practice: Part A: correct the tense in six sentences from your portfolio. Part B: label each verb present perfect, past simple or past continuous. Part C: rewrite two paragraphs so every tense fits its time marker. Check yourself: Parts A-C use your own six portfolio sentences and two portfolio paragraphs, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm every present-perfect verb links to now or an unfinished time (often with since, already, yet, or no specific past time given), every past-simple verb pairs with a finished-time word (yesterday, last week, in Unit 4), and every past-continuous verb sets the background scene for another action, usually with while or as (e.g., "While I was presenting, the class listened"). Watch especially for the mixed-time mistake in the commonMistake note - a finished-time word like yesterday should never appear with have/has + past participle.

grammar.title: First conditional and unless
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Use the first conditional to talk about a likely future result of an action.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
If + present simple, will + verb: "If you rehearse, you will feel calmer."
Unless means if not: "Unless you practise, you will forget your lines."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "If you will rehearse, you will feel calmer" adds an extra will; the if-clause stays in the present simple.
grammar.memoryTip: One will only, and it belongs in the result half of the sentence.
grammar.practice: Part A: complete six first-conditional sentences about your presentation. Part B: rewrite three if-not sentences using unless. Part C: fix the verb in two conditionals from a classmate's draft. Check yourself: Parts A-C use your own six presentation sentences and two sentences from a classmate's draft, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm every first-conditional sentence keeps the if-clause in the present simple and puts exactly one will in the result clause ("If you rehearse, you will feel calmer," not "If you will rehearse..."), and that Part B's unless-sentences keep the same present simple + will pattern while dropping any double negative (unless already means if not, so never write "unless you don't practise").

grammar.title: Relative clauses and clear questions
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Add detail with who, which and where, and ask precise questions to defend your ideas.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
who for people: "the classmate who reviewed my work"; which or that for things: "the source which proved my point"; where for places: "the market where prices are compared."
Questions: "Where did you find this evidence?"
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "the teacher which helped me" uses the wrong pronoun; people always take who, not which.
grammar.memoryTip: who names a person, which or that names a thing, and where names a place.
grammar.practice: Part A: join six sentence pairs with who, which or where. Part B: write six audience questions using Wh- words. Part C: correct the relative pronoun in two mixed-up sentences. Check yourself: Parts A-C use your own six sentence pairs, six audience questions and two mixed-up sentences, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm who joins a person, which or that joins a thing, and where joins a place, with the clause sitting right after the noun it describes (never "the teacher which helped me"), and confirm every Wh- question in Part B starts with a Wh- word and puts the auxiliary before the subject, matching "Where did you find this evidence?"

grammar.title: Precise description with adjectives and adverbs
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Strengthen your writing with participle adjectives, ordered adjectives and comparative adverbs.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The -ed form shows a feeling, the -ing form shows a cause: "I was excited by the exciting result."
Adjective order: opinion before fact, as in "a clever new idea."
Comparative adverb: "She spoke more clearly than before."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "I was exciting" when you mean "I was excited" swaps the forms; the -ing word describes what causes the feeling.
grammar.memoryTip: Use -ed for how you feel and -ing for the thing that causes it.
grammar.practice: Part A: choose the -ed or -ing adjective in six sentences. Part B: reorder the adjectives in four noun phrases. Part C: upgrade two plain verbs with a comparative adverb. Check yourself: Parts A-C use your own six sentences, four noun phrases and two upgraded verbs, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm each -ed adjective describes how someone feels and each -ing adjective describes what causes that feeling ("I was excited by the exciting result," never "I was exciting"), confirm each noun phrase orders opinion before fact (e.g., "a clever new idea"), and confirm each comparative adverb uses more + adverb followed by than ("spoke more clearly than before") rather than doubling a -er ending.

grammar.title: Joining ideas and reporting speech
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Connect your ideas smoothly and report accurately what other people said.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Connectives: and, but, because, so, while, until: "I revised my draft because feedback helped me."
Reported speech steps the verb back: "She said she had finished" from "I have finished."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "She said that she have finished" keeps the wrong verb; shift it one tense back to "had finished."
grammar.memoryTip: In reported speech, step the verb one tense further into the past.
grammar.practice: Part A: combine six idea pairs with a suitable connective. Part B: rewrite four quotations as reported speech. Part C: join two short sentences from your reflection. Check yourself: Parts A-C use your own six idea pairs, four quotations and two reflection sentences, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm each connective matches its logical job (and adds, but contrasts, because gives a reason, so gives a result, while/until mark time), and confirm each reported-speech rewrite steps the verb one tense further into the past, matching "She said she had finished" from "I have finished" - never leaving the original tense as in "She said that she have finished."

grammar.title: Final editing conference
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Proofread for compound nouns, pronouns, capital letters, spelling and punctuation.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Compound nouns can be closed (notebook), hyphenated (self-esteem) or open (bus stop).
Indefinite pronouns take a singular verb: "Everyone is ready."
Reflexive pronoun: "I checked the work myself."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "Everyone are ready" uses a plural verb; indefinite pronouns like everyone and nobody are singular.
grammar.memoryTip: Read your work aloud once for meaning and once again only for punctuation.
grammar.practice: Part A: fix the verb in six indefinite-pronoun sentences. Part B: write each compound noun in its correct closed, hyphenated or open form. Part C: run the final checklist over your whole capstone. Check yourself: Parts A-C proofread your own six indefinite-pronoun sentences, your own compound nouns and your whole capstone, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm every indefinite pronoun (everyone, nobody, somebody, everything, and similar words) takes a singular verb such as is, has or does ("Everyone is ready," never "Everyone are ready"), confirm each compound noun keeps a consistent closed, hyphenated or open form (notebook, self-esteem, bus stop), and confirm the final pass follows the memory tip - read once for meaning and once again only for punctuation.

quizzes.question: What does 'illegal' mean?
quizzes.options: Not allowed by the law or by the rules | The act of going into a place, or the way inside | A tool or device used to make music or do a job | The power to form fresh pictures and ideas in your mind
quizzes.correctAnswer: Not allowed by the law or by the rules
quizzes.explanation: Something illegal breaks the law or the agreed rules.

quizzes.question: What does 'citizen' mean?
quizzes.options: The power to make your own choices and take action | Connected to the physical features of the Earth and how places lie | A person who legally belongs to a country and shares its rights | At the beginning, or in the first place
quizzes.correctAnswer: A person who legally belongs to a country and shares its rights
quizzes.explanation: A citizen belongs to a country and shares its rights and duties.

quizzes.question: What does 'geographic' mean?
quizzes.options: Something that could cause harm or danger | Connected to the physical features of the Earth and how places lie | A ruler who holds complete power and makes every rule alone | A group of people and animals travelling together across a desert
quizzes.correctAnswer: Connected to the physical features of the Earth and how places lie
quizzes.explanation: Geographic features are the physical features of the Earth.

quizzes.question: What does 'originally' mean?

quizzes.question: What does 'treacherous' mean?

quizzes.question: What does 'explorer' mean?

liveSessions.agenda: 5 min check-in; 10 min model; 15 min workshop; 10 min conference or rehearsal; 5 min next step

teacherNotes.note: Conference at each milestone, verify responsible source use, preserve learner ownership, assess the researched product and four-minute presentation with shared rubrics, and record actionable Grade 7 transition feedback.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Confirm the learner chose one reading, one writing and one speaking piece from Units 1-9 and gave a clear reason for each choice.
Check that all thirty review words are sorted into sensible categories and that the learner can explain at least three of the links.
Verify the learner compared evidence from at least two approved course sources and noted where those sources agree or differ.
Confirm the learner gave three specific rubric-based suggestions and recorded the three suggestions they received in return.
Check the four-minute presentation was rehearsed twice and that pace, emphasis and transitions improved between the two runs.
Confirm the learner presented the product, answered at least three audience questions and recorded a specific Grade 7 learning goal.
Correct answer: Not allowed by the law or by the rules. Something illegal breaks the law or the agreed rules.
Correct answer: A person who legally belongs to a country and shares its rights. A citizen belongs to a country and shares its rights and duties.
Correct answer: Connected to the physical features of the Earth and how places lie. Geographic features are the physical features of the Earth.
Correct answer: At the beginning, or in the first place. Originally means at the very beginning.
Correct answer: Something that could cause harm or danger. A threat is something that could cause harm or danger.
Correct answer: Dangerous and unsafe, often because it is not what it seems. Treacherous ground is dangerous and not what it seems.
Correct answer: A narrow strip of sea joining two larger areas of water. Straits are a narrow strip of sea between two areas of water.
Correct answer: A person who travels to new places to discover things. An explorer travels to new places to discover things.
Correct answer: Modest, and not thinking you are better than other people. A humble person is modest and not boastful.
Correct answer: Straits. A strait is a narrow strip of sea between two areas of land, so 'straits' fits the sentence.
